stem.en: In Steward's experiment, single phloem cells from a carrot root grew into complete carrot plants. What does this tell us about the phloem cells of carrot?

text.en: They are totipotent: under the right conditions, one cell can grow into a whole plant.

feedback.en: Yes. A cell that can divide and then form every part of a new plant is a totipotent cell.

text.en: They are meristem cells, which go on dividing all the time while they are in the root.

feedback.en: No. Phloem is a permanent tissue. Its cells do not divide in the carrot; they divided again only in the nutrient medium.

text.en: They form a mass of cells, but a mass of phloem cells can only ever make more phloem.

feedback.en: No. The mass formed roots, a shoot and finally a whole plant, so it made many kinds of cell.

text.en: They grow into plants by themselves, so a carrot kept on a kitchen shelf forms new plants.

feedback.en: No. The cells divided only in a nutrient medium with sugars and hormones, in suitable conditions.

explanation.en: The phloem cells of carrot are totipotent. Inside the carrot they do not divide, but in a nutrient medium they regained the ability to divide, formed a mass of cells, and then formed roots, a shoot and a whole plant. This happened only under specific conditions, in a medium with sugars and hormones.

hints.en: What is the name for the ability of one cell to grow into a whole plant?
